claim: Collar carries about 0.99 kN holding a 100 kg person with the victim set
law: Weight = m g (100 kg person, 0.96 kg of triangle, sling and carabiner)
check: claimed 0.99 kN, estimate 0.99 kN (ratio 1.00)

claim: A drop of up to 30 mm onto the rope when the feet are freed stays inside the frame's strength margin
law: Energy balance of a rigid mass on 1 m of rope, F = W (1 + sqrt(1 + 2 k h / W)); 4 % stretch (CAL) and the stiffest plausible rope, 2 %; frame limit 2.5 kN x 1.36 (the bars' combined factor, [C1b])
check: 30 mm of slack: 2.6 kN (4 %) to 3.0 kN (2 %), above the 2.5 kN of R1 but inside 3.4 kN; 100 mm with 2 % rope: 4.3 kN, beyond it. The 30 mm is a drill limit, not physics (independent review); to close: the drill caps slack and the TRL 4 proof load is raised above 3 kN (TKB-DEC-001 O7)

claim: The collar locks on wet bark: combined friction of pads and sleeved chain at least 0.58 on a 200 mm trunk (0.9 assumed)
law: Self-locking couple: lock if (mu_pad + mu_chain) >= h / e (TKB-CAL-001 section 3); friction of rubber and nylon on wet coconut bark is not published
check: needed 0.58, assumed 0.9 (0.5 + 0.4), locking factor 1.54; no measured value; to close: friction on wet bark measured at TRL 4 (BLD-001 first check 1)

claim: The simplified lock condition h / e in the CAL is on the safe side of the full equilibrium
law: Moments about the trunk axis with the pad contacts at r cos 30 deg, the chain at R_c on the far side and the two pad normals (friction mu N / cos 30 deg); same frictions as S3

claim: The frame settles less than the 20 mm of R1 at 2.5 kN
law: Pad squash at a 6 MPa compression modulus plus one link of chain seating, levered by e / h (TKB-CAL-001 [B5]); the independent review adds shear of the pads under their share of the vertical friction (G about 1.1 MPa) and tilt of the chain at the back
check: 10 mm in the CAL; about 13 mm with pad shear, 14 to 18 mm with chain tilt, against 20 mm; to close: settlement measured in the TRL 4 proof test

claim: Bearing bars stay below the welded (heat-affected) proof strength of 6082-T6 at 2.5 kN
law: RHS 50 x 40 x 3 from the spine: bending in plan, vertical bending from the pad's friction and torsion from the bottom-edge contact, combined by von Mises (independent review); f0,haz = 125 MPa (EN 1999-1-1 values for welded 6082-T6)
check: 92 MPa <= 125 MPa

claim: Bar to spine fillet welds stay below the weld metal strength
law: Weld group in bending, 5 mm fillets (3.5 mm throat) all round; ER5356 weld metal 210 MPa; about 57 MPa equivalent with the shear (independent review), still factor 3.7
check: 40 MPa <= 210 MPa

claim: The load eye does not tear out at 2.5 kN
law: Two shear planes through the 13 mm eye stack (spine and doubler rings), 14 mm of edge beyond the 22 mm eye, 0.577 x 185 MPa HAZ ultimate

claim: The 5 mm cleat web beside a slot stays below the welded proof strength with all of the chain's pull on one slot (450 mm trunk)
law: Ligament in bending beside the slot, web 55 mm deep (D-S2); the two legs need not share the tension (capstan ratio about 6 round the wrap), so the worst case puts it all on one slot; with the old 35 mm web this case gave 162 MPa (factor 0.77) and failed; f0,haz = 125 MPa
check: 103 MPa <= 125 MPa

claim: Steel chain links bearing on the aluminium slot faces do not wear or dent the cleat in service
law: Projected bearing of a 6 mm link on the 5 mm web against about 1.5 x f0,haz; local line contact and repeated use make wear the open question
check: projected bearing 92 MPa against about 190 MPa; wear and denting not calculable on paper; to close: inspect the slot faces after the TRL 4 proof tests (TKB-DEC-001 item 11)

claim: The 6 mm grade 80 chain holds the largest chain tension with a wide margin
law: Grade 80, 6 mm: minimum breaking force 45.2 kN, working load limit 1.12 t (S3i, EN 818-2 class); checked with all of the pull in one leg (independent review); a link bearing on a flat web is not the link-on-link case of the rating, a reason the factor is kept large

claim: The rope at its figure-eight loop holds 2.5 kN wet, with margin
law: Basis here: EN 1891 type A holds 15 kN for 3 minutes with figure-eight terminations, less 15 % wet (the CAL's [C6] uses 22 kN x 0.65 knot efficiency, 14.3 kN dry); new-rope values, so abrasion and descender bends are left to the retirement rules (S26)
closed_by: TKB-CAL-001 [C6] (14 kN dry at the knot)

claim: Brake hand force for a 100 kg person stays under the 150 N of R5
law: Capstan friction T1/T2 = exp(mu theta): rope on aluminium mu 0.2 over 540 deg in the descender and 180 deg over the brake carabiner; cross-check: EN 341 limits the holding force to 200 N at the device's maximum rated load (150 kg for the cited class), about 135 N at 101 kg, 72 N with the brake carabiner. Within for a certified device on dry rope: the capstan estimate reaches 150 N at a friction of 0.15 and 282 N at 0.10 (independent review)

claim: Lowering 100 kg through 25 m turns 24.8 kJ into heat; the descender warms by 44 K at most
law: Energy balance m g h = heat in the descender, brake carabiner and hand; dT = Q / (m c), 0.53 kg of aluminium, c 900 J/(kg K): bulk rise 44 K, the body near 79 C from 35 C ambient, hotter at the rope contact; the hand holds only the handle and the brake strand (S29); EN 341 class A allows 7.5 x 10^6 J of descent energy
check: in 24.75 kJ, out 24.76 kJ

claim: 30 m of rope lowers from 25 m
law: Rope used = 25 m drop + 1 m to the person + 1.5 m of knots + 0.5 m round the brake carabiner

claim: The 110-link chain fits every trunk from 200 to 450 mm and leaves at least 4 links in the adjustable tail
law: Chain path round the trunk from the model: loop links + fixed end + tail = 110; links counted on the 450 mm trunk; on a 200 mm trunk 59 links (about 1.1 m) hang free and are stowed in the bag's clip loop
check: 15 links >= 4 links

claim: A trained climber fixes the collar and clips the victim in under 5 minutes once in position
law: Task time estimate summed step by step (TKB-CAL-001 [E3]); work at height on a climbing device, hot and possibly wet
check: estimate 4.5 min against 5 min; a thin margin, no timed drill yet; to close: timed drill at 3 m at TRL 4 (BLD-001 first checks; PR-004)

claim: The rescuer carries under 5 kg up the trunk
law: Sum of the carried items from the model and catalogue masses, with the cited descender at 600 g (Petzl I'D S class) and the 55 mm cleat web of D-S2

claim: The rubber pads do not crush the bark at 2.5 kN
law: Pad pressure from the CAL against the compressive strength of coconut stem wood, 9.28 MPa air dry at 400 kg/m3 average density (Rana et al. 2015; grain direction as reported); green or wet wood is typically 40 to 50 % weaker, and a cocked pad bears on a strip near its lower edge (independent review)
check: 1.9 MPa mean, about 3.8 MPa at the lower edge, against about 4.6 to 5.6 MPa green; no margin left at the edge; to close: crush test on green stem sections at TRL 4

claim: Bare chain links outside the sleeve mark the bark less than the 5 mm of R8 (static)
law: Line load T / R = 23 N/mm on a 6 mm wire; the wire sinks until the contact width w = q / 9.28 MPa (2.5 mm); depth = r - sqrt(r^2 - (w/2)^2); static only: dragging while tightening is not included; about 1.4 mm on green wood at 4.6 MPa

claim: The collar does not penetrate the stem and leaves no mark deeper than 5 mm
law: Palms have no vascular cambium, so any mark is permanent (Broschat 2019): the shallow static marks of S20 stay; the collar has no spikes, screws or cleats; pad crushing depends on S19 (reworded after the independent review)
check: no penetrating part; marks about 0.3 to 1.3 mm static; to close: bark inspection after the TRL 4 lowerings (PR-008)

claim: The victim turns head up in the triangle once the feet are freed
law: Statics: a hanging body settles with its centre of mass below the attachment; the triangle and chest sling attach at the hips and chest, above the centre of mass when head up
check: attachment above the centre of mass when head up, but hanging head down from the hips is also a stable state; that the body passes from one to the other unaided is not shown by statics (independent review); to close: dummy drill at TRL 4

claim: The kit brings a stranded climber down in minutes, against the 30 to 150 minutes reported
law: Rigging (S17) + lowering 25 m at 0.3 m/s + about 3 minutes to climb to the victim (not timed); reported waits from the PRB sources
check: about 9 min against 30 to 150 min; rests on S17 and an untimed climb; to close: timed drill at TRL 4

claim: The upward pull of R2 does not arise when the collar is at least 300 mm above the victim's attachment
law: The load strand runs from the descender down to the attachment point below it, so the force on the load eye points down; the upward case needs the attachment above the collar (the drill rule, decision 16A). A victim 0.3 m to the side on 1 m of rope adds about 0.3 W sideways, not counted in the lock analysis (independent review)
check: -1 (vertical component of the rope pull, up positive, per unit load) <= 0 (vertical component of the rope pull, up positive, per unit load)
closed_by: TKB-DDR-003 16A; R2 stays at risk on the drill, not on the physics

claim: Bare 6082-T6 frame in contact with steel chain, zinc-plated keeper and stainless screws survives humid coastal use
law: Aluminium is anodic to steel and stainless steel in a wet joint; the pad screws sit in stainless rivet nuts with barrier paste, the chain touches the slots only while rigged, and the kit is stored dry in its bag
check: galvanic attack needs a standing electrolyte; the controls are in the build plan; the rate on bare 6082 in sea air is not calculated; to close: inspect the frame after the TRL 4 trial season (TKB-RSK-001 FMEA)

claim: Rope, webbing and rubber pads keep their properties in tropical sun and heat for their service life
law: Polyamide and natural rubber degrade in UV and ozone; the kit is stored in its bag out of the sun, and rope, slings and pads are retired on the makers' inspection rules
check: time-dependent; controlled by storage and inspection, not by a margin; to close: makers' retirement rules adopted in the drill card at TRL 4 (TKB-RSK-001)

claim: The tether link threads the chain's end link: wire diameter inside the 6 mm grade 80 link's 7.8 mm opening
law: Inner width of 6 mm grade 80 chain at least 7.8 mm (S3i, EN 818-2 class); the BOM's 8 mm quick link failed this check and was replaced by a 6 mm grade 80 connecting link (7 mm at the chain end) through a 10 mm tether hole
check: 7 mm <= 7.3 mm
closed_by: TKB-DEC-001 D-S1 (fix under the standing instruction)

claim: The brake carabiner has the 22 mm spare eye to itself, clear of the tether
law: D3 model interference check (cad/fidelity.json) after D-S1: the tether link and the fixed end of the chain sit in front of the spine, the brake carabiner alone in the spare eye
check: 0 mm3 of overlap <= 5 mm3 of overlap

claim: The brake strand the rescuer holds stays far below the 48 C touch limit of EN 341
law: 8 % of the 24.8 kJ goes into the hand and the brake strand running through it; spread over the 1.95 kg of rope that passes the hand (c about 1.7 kJ/(kg K)) it warms the rope by about this much; limit: 48 C less 35 C ambient. The descender body (85 %, up to 44 K) is held only by its handle

claim: The collar's static system safety factor on a one-person load sits within the 5:1 to 10:1 that rope rescue teams aim for
law: Breaking load estimated from the weakest frame member at the welded ultimate strength, over the 0.99 kN working load; rescue practice ratios 5:1 to 10:1, 15:1 once common (Piatt 2023); EN 795 tests anchor devices statically at 12 kN
check: 5.0 kN with the chain's pull shared (5.1:1, the bars govern), 4.5 kN with all of it on one slot (4.5:1): below 5:1 in the worst case. Amish decided on 2026-10-25 (TKB-DEC-001 O7, option C): keep the 2.5 kN design load, raise the TRL 4 proof load to 3.5 kN and decide after a test to failure of a sample frame, with the stronger frame (option B) as the recorded fallback if it shows less than 5:1
closed_by: Test to failure of a sample frame and the 3.5 kN proof test, TRL 4 (TKB-DEC-001 O7)

claim: The collar locks on a trunk leaning up to 20 deg with the frame on either side
law: Self-locking condition on a leaning trunk, frame on the adverse side: need = h cos t / (e cos t - h sin t) (independent review), 200 mm trunk, the same assumed friction 0.9
check: locking factor 1.30 at 15 deg, 1.21 at 20 deg, 1.02 at 30 deg on the adverse side; Amish decided on 2026-10-25 (TKB-DEC-001 O8, option C): a 20 deg lean limit in PR-003 and a drill rule that sets the frame on the favourable side of a leaning trunk; to close: friction test and the drill on a leaning palm

claim: The tether hole holds the fixed end's share of the chain tension if the keeper is unseated
law: Two shear planes of the 7 mm web strip beside the 10 mm tether hole, 5 mm thick, 0.577 x 185 MPa HAZ ultimate, against the chain tension at the R1 load (2.2 kN at the working load); the tether is not a working load path
closed_by: TKB-DEC-001 D-S1 (factor 1.4 at the R1 load, 3.4 at the working load)

claim: Option B: a strap wrapped 4 turns and tied off as a Klemheist holds 2.5 kN along a vertical 300 mm trunk
law: Capstan friction over the wrapped length: axial holding about 2 pi n mu T with the band tension T at least W / 2 in each wrap (mu 0.3 assumed, polyester on wet bark); friction hitches round large trunks under axial load are not covered by a cited source
check: holding about 3.8 times the load on paper; the self-tightening of the hitch round a large, wet, tapering trunk is the open question; not carried forward (option B is not carried forward unless Amish chooses it)

claim: Option B: the 45 mm polyester anchor strap holds 2.5 kN with margin
law: EN 795 anchor devices are tested statically at 12 kN (metallic) or 18 kN (textile, no service-life marking) for one user (EN 795 summary, Vandernet)

claim: Option B: the wraps press the bark far below its crushing strength
law: Band pressure p = T / (R w) at T = W / 2 on a 300 mm trunk, 45 mm webbing, against 9.28 MPa (Rana et al. 2015)

claim: Option B: a climber ties the 4-turn wrap at height in about 90 s
law: Task time estimate: four wraps and a Klemheist with a 4 m strap, one hand on the trunk
check: estimate 90 s against 60 s for the collar; not timed; not carried forward (option B)

claim: Option C: four M10 x 120 coach screws hold 2.5 kN in the stem
law: Johansen steel-plate-to-timber estimate per screw with timber formulas (EN 1995-1-1 form) at 400 kg/m3: 8.6 kN each; palm stem wood is fibre bundles in soft tissue, not timber, so the embedment strength is unknown
check: about 35 kN for four screws on timber formulas against 2.5 kN; not valid for palm wood without a test; not carried forward (option C is not carried forward unless Amish chooses it)

claim: Option C: four 10 mm holes 110 mm deep do not seriously harm the palm
law: Palm stem wounds are permanent (Broschat 2019); every use leaves four more holes, an entry for pests and rot; R8 limits marks to 5 mm
check: the holes are permanent and fail R8 by design; harm to the palm is not quantified; not carried forward (option C); fails PR-008 by design

claim: Option C: the 10 mm steel eye lug does not tear out at 2.5 kN
law: Two shear planes of the 10 mm lug below the 22 mm hole (39 mm of material), 0.577 x 410 MPa ultimate (S275 class)

claim: Option C: driving four coach screws by hand at height fits the 5 minutes of R4
law: Pilot drilling and driving 4 x 120 mm screws with a ratchet while hanging on a climbing device, estimate 2 min a screw
check: estimate about 8 min for the screws alone against 5 min for the whole rig; not carried forward (option C); at risk against PR-004
